justice: The street allocates most visible space to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while pedestrian space appears limited to narrow edge sidewalks.
A central planted median and side green strips provide some shared public-space value, but they do not directly improve access for all users as much as wider sidewalks or crossings would.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crosswalks, or pedestrian refuge features can be identified in the image, weakening accessibility and fairness for non-drivers.
Streetlights are regularly spaced along both sides, suggesting some even distribution of basic infrastructure across the corridor.
The corridor appears highly driver-oriented, so spatial benefits are not distributed equally among walkers, cyclists, and transit users.
safety: Fresh lane markings, wide lanes, and a straight alignment support predictable vehicle movement and reduce immediate crash risk for drivers.
A raised landscaped median separates opposing traffic streams, improving safety by reducing head-on conflict potential.
Curbs and planted buffers create some separation between the main carriageway and side areas, helping organize movement.
However, the road is very wide and appears designed for higher speeds, which can increase severity of crashes for any crossing pedestrian or cyclist.
No visible marked pedestrian crossing, traffic-calming device, or dedicated protected cycle track is present in the scene.
livability: The corridor has very low visible street activity, with few people, shops, or social destinations present along the roadway.
Large construction fencing on the left and open undeveloped land on the right reduce the sense of an active, everyday neighborhood environment.
The broad road profile prioritizes through traffic over street life, making the space feel more infrastructural than community-oriented.
Grass medians and roadside planting add some environmental quality, but they do not compensate for the lack of human-scale amenities.
No benches, bus-stop shelters, storefronts, or gathering spaces are visible, limiting support for daily social use.
sustainability: The landscaped median and green verges introduce permeable planted areas that modestly support stormwater absorption and urban greening.
Street lighting and orderly roadway design suggest a relatively modern corridor that may support durable infrastructure performance.
There is no visible dedicated bus lane, bus stop, or high-quality transit interface in the image, so sustainable mode support appears limited.
No protected bicycle lane or bicycle parking is visible, reducing encouragement for low-carbon travel choices.

aesthetics: The road surface is clean and newly paved, giving the corridor a tidy and well-maintained appearance.
The central green median and side grass strips soften the otherwise hard roadway and improve visual order.
Streetlights are consistently spaced and the corridor geometry is visually coherent, creating a neat formal streetscape.
Construction cranes, fenced worksites, and large vacant edges reduce visual richness and make parts of the scene feel unfinished.

comfort: Thermal comfort is limited because the corridor has almost no visible shade trees or canopy cover over sidewalks and cycling space.

Physical comfort for pedestrians is weaker because the visible side path is narrow and exposed, with no benches or rest facilities.
Psychological comfort may be moderate for drivers because the road is uncluttered and well organized, but lower for non-drivers because of the wide, fast-feeling traffic environment.
The green median and verge planting slightly improve visual and microclimatic comfort, though not enough to offset the highly exposed setting.
walkability: A sidewalk or edge path is visible on the right side, but it appears narrow relative to the overall road width and lacks pedestrian-focused amenities.
No marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or refuge islands are visible in the image, making route continuity across the corridor uncertain.
The street is very wide and speed-oriented, which generally discourages walking even if a side path exists.
There are no visible storefronts, entrances, seating areas, or active frontages to make walking interesting or useful for daily needs.
Lack of shade trees and shelters reduces walking comfort, especially in hot or rainy conditions.
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bicycle lane is visible on either side of the roadway.
The broad carriageway and likely higher traffic speeds create a stressful environment for on-road cycling.
Curbs and medians organize traffic, but they do not provide a safe cycling facility or buffer specifically for cyclists.
No bicycle markings, bike boxes, or bicycle parking infrastructure can be identified in the scene.
The smooth pavement could support cycling physically, but the absence of clear cycling infrastructure keeps overall bikeability low.
